'''George Ogurek Zimmerman''' (October 20, 1935 &ndash; May 6, 2019) was a Polish-born American scientist, researcher, inventor, professor of physics and physics department chair at [[Boston University]]. Zimmerman achieved his PhD in solid state physics in 1963 at [[Yale University]] and came to Boston University in the fall of 1963.

Zimmerman's major contributions in physics include discoveries in Condensed Matter and Solid State Physics, phase transitions at ultra low temperatures, magnetically intercalated graphite compounds, Jahn-Teller materials, and applied [[superconductivity]] and modeling.<ref name=APS>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/units/fhp/governance/elections/candidates.cfm#zimmerman |title=APS Physics &#124; FHP &#124; Election 2010 Candidate Biographies |publisher=Aps.org |date= |access-date=2014-03-10}}</ref>
Zimmerman is also well known for his popular lectures on physics, hands-on advanced laboratory lectures and, a Summer Research Internship Program for High School students.<ref name="APS" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bu.edu/summer/high-school-programs/research-internship/timeline.shtml |title=High School Summer Research Internship in Science & Engineering History & Timeline At BU Summer Term |publisher=Bu.edu |date= |access-date=2014-03-10 |archive-date=2014-03-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310171210/http://www.bu.edu/summer/high-school-programs/research-internship/timeline.shtml }}</ref>

Zimmerman's accomplishments were highlighted in the 17th edition of Who's Who in the World, the 7th through 10th editions of Who's Who in Science and Engineering, and multiple editions of Who's Who in America published between 1986 and 2016. He resided in Boston, where he enjoyed classical music and photography and pursued his research in physics and history until the end of his life.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.24-7pressrelease.com/press-release/dr-george-zimmerman-honored-for-excellence-as-a-physicist-professor-and-researcher-424388.php |title=Dr. George Zimmerman Honored for Excellence as a Physicist, Professor and Researcher |publisher=24-7 Press Release |date= |access-date=2017-01-14}}</ref> Zimmerman died at the age of 83 in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bostonglobe/obituary.aspx?n=george-o-zimmerman&pid=192816638&fhid=5816 |title=Boston Globe Obituaries |publisher=Legacy.com |date= |access-date=2019-05-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/brookline-ma/george-zimmerman-8273653|title=George Zimmerman Obituary - Brookline, MA|website=Dignity Memorial}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
George Ogurek Zimmerman was born  on October 20, 1935, in Poland.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7g1LAQAAIAAJ&q=%22George+Ogurek%22+1935|title = Who's who in Science and Engineering|year = 2008|isbn = 978-0-8379-5768-5 | last1=Marquis | first1=Who's Who | last2=Who | first2=Marquis Who's | publisher=Marquis Who's Who }}</ref> He received his Ph.D. in Physics from [[Yale University]] in 1963. His thesis was in experimental low temperature physics.

After a few months as a post-doc with C.T. Lane at Yale, he joined the Physics Department at [[Boston University]]<ref name="APS" /> His research interests are in Condensed Matter and Solid State Physics. More specifically, some of the topics of interest are phase transitions, some at ultra low temperatures, magnetically intercalated graphite compounds, Jahn-Teller materials, and applied superconductivity and modeling. At Boston University, Zimmerman was department chair for 12 years, chaired the Faculty Council, and was a member and chair of several other influential university committees.

His research collaborations include the Francis Bitter National Magnet Laboratory at [[MIT]], and sabbaticals at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], [[University of California, San Diego|UC San Diego]], [[Leiden University]], the Netherlands, [[Harvard University]], Cambridge US, and [[Imperial College]], London.

He was a Member At Large of the Governing Board of the Forum on the History of Physics (FHP) and its Webmaster ad hoc. He conducted many oral history interviews<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories|title=American Institute of Physics: Oral History Interviews|last=|first=|date=|website=www.aip.org|access-date=2019-09-17}}</ref> which have been archived at the Niels Bohr Library and Archives at the [[American Institute of Physics]].

He established a Summer Research Internship Program for High School students starting in the early 1980s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bu.edu/summer/high-school-programs/rise-internship-practicum|title=RISE Internship / Practicum|last=|first=|date=|website=www.bu.edu|access-date=2024-07-18}}</ref>

==Inventions==
Zimmerman has developed high temperature superconductor based high current [[Lead (electronics)|leads]], which became the first industrial application of the then newly discovered high temperature ceramic superconductors.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsearch-bool.html&r=1&f=G&l=50&co1=AND&d=PTXT&s1=5,376,755.PN.&OS=PN/5,376,755&RS=PN/5,376,755 |title=Composite lead for conducting an electric current between 75-80K and 4.5K temperatures |publisher=patft.uspto.gov |date= |access-date=2014-02-02 }}</ref>
Some of Zimmerman's inventions were granted a patent as listed here (patent number and title):
* 5,399,547  Method for increasing the critical current density of high transition temperature superconductors  
* 5,376,755  Composite lead for conducting an electric current between 75-80K and 4.5K temperatures  
* 5,296,459  Method for making an electrically conductive contact for joining high T<sub>c</sub> superconductors.      
* 5,131,582  Adhesive metallic alloys and methods of their use  
* 5,098,656  Alloys for electrically joining superconductors to themselves, to normal conductors, and to semi-conductors  
* 4,966,142  Method for electrically joining superconductors to themselves, to normal conductors, and to semi-conductors
* 4,837,377  Rubbery, Electrically Non-Conductive, and Intrinsically Magnetic Graphite Intercalation Compounds and Methods for Their Making
